title: Anglicans
hook: the Church of England and its worldwide family: a middle way, the Book of Common Prayer

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was chief end: glorify God, and enjoy him. Your line was god is sovereign.

These words turn up at weddings, even for people who never set foot in a church: dearly beloved, we are gathered together here. For better, for worse, for richer, for poorer, in sickness and in health. And at funerals: earth to earth, ashes to ashes, dust to dust. Those lines, give or take a word, come from one book, shaped above all by one man, an archbishop named Thomas Cranmer, in the 1540s and 50s. He was later burned at the stake for his faith. His book taught generations to pray in their own language, and quietly shaped English itself. It's called the Book of Common Prayer. Common, as in shared: the same prayers, said together, by everyone.
screen: `FOR BETTER, FOR WORSE.` → `ASHES TO ASHES.` → `ONE BOOK, PRAYED IN COMMON.`

segments.voice: Anglicans are the Church of England and the worldwide churches that grew from it: the Episcopal Church in the United States, the Church of Nigeria, the Church of Uganda, the Anglican Church of Australia and many more, with large and growing churches in Africa. The break with Rome came under King Henry the Eighth in the 1530s, tangled up with his marriage and politics as much as faith. But under Cranmer, and later Queen Elizabeth the First, the church found its own shape. Anglicans came to call it a middle way: Catholic in its bishops, creeds and sacraments; Reformed in its stress on scripture, grace, and worship in the people's own language. Some lean toward the Catholic side, with incense and vestments; some toward the evangelical, with preaching and plain services. They share one book of prayer, in many languages. One small form runs all through it: the collect. That's COL-lect, stress on the first syllable, a short prayer that gathers the people's prayers into one sentence. It usually names God, remembers something God has done, asks, and ends through Christ. Here's one from the start of the 1662 communion service: "Almighty God, unto whom all hearts be open, all desires known, and from whom no secrets are hid: Cleanse the thoughts of our hearts by the inspiration of thy Holy Spirit, that we may perfectly love thee, and worthily magnify thy holy Name; through Christ our Lord. Amen." One sentence. That's the Anglican genius: large things said in few, careful words.
screen: `A WORLDWIDE FAMILY, STRONG IN AFRICA.` · `CATHOLIC AND REFORMED: A MIDDLE WAY.` · `THE COLLECT: ONE GATHERING SENTENCE.` · `UNTO WHOM ALL HEARTS BE OPEN.` · then, large: `FROM WHOM NO SECRETS ARE HID.`

segments.voice: If you pray, say the Collect for Purity slowly, a phrase per breath: Almighty God, unto whom all hearts be open, all desires known, and from whom no secrets are hid. Stop there, nothing hidden; add the rest if you wish. If you don't pray, sit with the idea of being fully known, and not turned away.
Anglicans. The Church of England and its worldwide family, praying from the Book of Common Prayer, walking a middle way.
Your line: a middle way. Catholic and Reformed, in one book. Day two hundred ninety-one, in the books.

howItsDone: Anglicans worship from a prayer book, with set prayers, readings and collects for each Sunday; many churches say Morning and Evening Prayer daily and celebrate Holy Communion weekly.

fork.setup: you're Thomas Cranmer in the 1540s. most of England's worship is in Latin, which most people don't understand. what do you do?
options: keep it in Latin, it's tradition.
write a book of prayer in English for everyone to say together.
let each church make up its own.
fork.reveal: Cranmer wrote the Book of Common Prayer in English, the same prayers for everyone. its words still echo at weddings and funerals.

original.note: Latin: a gathering. The collect gathers up the people's prayers into one short prayer.

trapdoor: what you thought: Anglicans are the English version of Catholics.
what it means: a worldwide family, strong in Africa, that holds Catholic and Reformed together, praying from a common book.
what a scholar hears: Cranmer's prose, from 1549 to 1662, and the collect, a Latin form he turned into English sentences people still pray.

notes: Editor review (282-299 pass): hook no longer tells the listener what they've heard; Cranmer 'shaped' rather than 'wrote' the book; cut 'millions', 'tens of millions, most of them now in Africa' and the 'most Anglicans live in Africa' myth (unsourced statistic), replaced with a myth on Henry VIII's motives; 'especially loved' collect softened.

The hook's wedding and funeral lines are given loosely ('give or take a word'); they are not marked as exact quotations. The 1662 burial text reads 'earth to earth, ashes to ashes, dust to dust'. Confirm.
Cranmer burned in 1556 under Mary I. Book of Common Prayer 1549, 1552, 1559, 1662.

Anglican Communion: about 85 million members, most in Africa (Nigeria, Uganda, etc.). Script says 'tens of millions'. Some Anglican churches (e.g. GAFCON-aligned) have strained relations with Canterbury; not mentioned.
'Middle way' (via media) as a self-description: the phrase is later (19th century) but describes the Elizabethan settlement. Confirm.
Collect for Purity quoted from 1662; please verify exact wording and capitalization ('holy Name').
